findings.summary: Three of the eleven labels are not printed in display.rs, so the drift test as written fails, and the 'requirements' label is printed nowhere.
findings.evidence: Read: 'throughput ' is formatted in crates/athena-core/src/status.rs:897 and 'checks     ' in status.rs:579, not in display.rs. display.rs:1162-1164 prints StatusView.next under the label 'next'. The plan keeps display.rs unchanged and puts spec gaps only in `next` lines, so 'requirements' never appears in athena status output. Fix: Make the drift test look for each label in either display.rs or status.rs. Drop the 'requirements' label and have measures for the status listing say 'status: next' (the label actually printed), or say the table includes labels that come from status.rs.

findings.summary: Speed is judged by where a requirement is displayed, which is a proxy for what the requirement is about.
findings.evidence: is_speed is true only when the measure's label is 'throughput' or 'checks'. A speed requirement that is checked by a test ('status: not shown'), or whose measure is 'none' because nothing meets it yet, would get Normal priority, which is exactly the case where urgency matters. Fix: Have the xtask test require that any requirement citing the 'Speed first' or 'Athena owns acceleration' heading has a throughput or checks measure, so the speed class cannot drift silently. Or say in the spec header that a speed requirement must use one of those two labels.

findings.summary: One 'next' line per gap could bury the other 'next' items when many requirements say none.
findings.evidence: display.rs:1162 prints every entry of v.next. The plan's own risks section says the number of 'none' mechanisms is unknown and may be large. Fix: Show a count plus the first few ids in 'next' (speed gaps first), and keep the full list in StatusView.spec_gaps so tests can still check all of it.

findings.summary: The cap only spreads the queueing over several passes; every gap is still queued in the end.
findings.evidence: Open requests block re-queueing, so each later pass queues 5 more until every gap has an open request. Fix: Keep the cap, but say in the CHANGELOG that it limits how fast requests are queued, not how many.

summary: I read the plan against xtask/tests/spec.rs, hestia.rs, status.rs, display.rs, BRIEF.md and docs/spec.toml, and its main claims check out. BRIEF.md has the heading "2026-10-13: Athena owns acceleration" at line 494, before "# Project Olympus" at line 550, and "2026-10-25: Speed first" at line 1069, after the LAST_DATE cut. docs/spec.toml has 135 requirements, and the only one mentioning "faster" is the learning-effectiveness requirement at line 928. So adding OLY-A-22 and OLY-A-23 with two pinned headings is a fair, narrow way to meet criterion 7, and the plan also updates the test at spec.rs:439 that would otherwise break. toml_edit is already a dependency of athena-core. review_passes (hestia.rs:1410) is the right place for a pass that queues requests. athena_in, queue and close all exist, and the "status" test filter matches a test in hestia.rs whose name contains "status". The demonstrations call the real code and each would fail without the behavior. I found no blocker or major problem. The plan is wrong about where some status labels are printed: "throughput" and "checks" are printed from athena-core/src/status.rs, not display.rs, and the new spec gaps appear under "next", not under a "requirements" heading. So the drift test as written would fail, and a "status: requirements" measure would name a heading that athena status never prints. Classing speed by the measure's label is a proxy, but it reads data written into the spec and is tested, so it is acceptable. The cap of 5 per pass only spreads out the queueing. Listing every gap as a "next" line could crowd out the other "next" items.
